title: Cloudflare WriteGuard Brings Fine-Grained Security Controls for MCP Servers
gist: Cloudflare introduced WriteGuard, a private-beta shared policy, attribution and auditing layer that sits behind its MCP server portal to control the write actions AI agents can perform. It assigns each tool a risk tier, uses existing OAuth identity rather than separate agent accounts, and sends scrubbed events to a centralized audit log.

insights.claim: WriteGuard is a shared policy, attribution and auditing layer that intercepts all incoming MCP requests behind Cloudflare's MCP server portal, loading the policy for the targeted tool and evaluating request context to allow or block it, with allowed-but-failed and denied requests routed to auditing.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A gateway-level control point for agent write actions addresses the core risk of agents modifying data via MCP.

insights.claim: WriteGuard defines tool-specific policies without requiring changes to the MCP server itself and serves as a shared security layer across all MCP servers connected through the Cloudflare portal, avoiding reimplementing controls per server for GitLab, Jira, wikis and Google Workspace.
insights.speaker: Scott Roe-Meschke
insights.so_what: Centralizing controls avoids inconsistent per-server security implementations as MCP server count grows.
insights.quote: Reimplementing them in each server would take more work and produce inconsistent behavior.

insights.claim: WriteGuard assigns each tool a risk tier from read-only up to critical, classifying operations like completing a merge request, triggering a production deployment, or bulk-deleting records as critical, while creating a merge request or updating an issue field is a contained write and marking a notification read is minimal.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A tiered risk taxonomy gives teams a structured way to gate agent actions by blast radius.
insights.locator: Each tool is assigned a risk tier paragraph

themes.theme: Identity and audit without separate agent accounts

insights.claim: WriteGuard does not require standalone agent accounts, which would create a second set of permissions to manage, and instead uses existing OAuth credentials to identify the user while adding MCP client and session context to the human identity.
insights.speaker: Scott Roe-Meschke
insights.so_what: Anchoring agent actions to human identity keeps audit trails coherent without doubling permission management.
insights.quote: create a second set of permissions to manage
insights.locator: WriteGuard does not require creating standalone agent accounts paragraph

insights.claim: WriteGuard classifies each invocation as successful, failed, or blocked and asynchronously sends a scrubbed event omitting secret or sensitive values to an internal audit Worker, including server, tool, risk tier, outcome, user, client, and duration.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Structured scrubbed audit events make agent activity investigable without leaking secrets.
